blocks.1: Dahl writes in the 1824 article, p. 504: “..beneath this last-named cross a very clear spring wells up, straight out of the ground, and according to legend it is a holy spring.” From what I have read about this spring, it seems that almost everyone thinks it may be a holy spring from the earliest times. Many call it a sacrificial spring and connect it with the sacrificial grove they believe lay below, on the parsonage bog. Here Dahl found, as he wrote himself, when he had the bog drained, “a great number of unrotted, whole and intact, enormous oak trunks..” He goes on: “The swamp had thus formed because of the mass of unused timber, which prevented the water from draining away..” This, then, is the background to what is told about there being soft bog here in older times – indeed I have also heard open water.
blocks.2: Bishop Neumann in Bergen wrote in “Budstikken” (1824) about an official journey to Sogn and Sunnfjord in 1823, among other things: “Here on the parsonage land, where legend speaks of a mighty sacrificial grove, whose old oaks have even been found in a bog that Dahl has had dug out below the sacrificial spring, which is still shown, it is most likely that the assembly stood, as at the most solemn place.” He also writes: “Olaf the Holy had a church built here, probably on the same site where the present one stands.”
blocks.3: Dahl finds it strange that these fine oak logs, which lay so close and so handy, and which there must have been great use for in those times of scarce timber, had not been used. He asks, among other things, whether the reason might be that the Christians felt revulsion for heathendom, or whether it was superstition that kept the oaks from being used. (As mentioned earlier, many believe that this sacrificial grove was cut down in connection with the “rendering harmless” of other heathen symbols when the people were baptised at the Gulating.) Dahl writes further, p. 505: “Might not this grove have been connected with the spring where the stone cross stands, and the whole have marked a heathen sacrificial site or the place where offerings or slaughter took place, a place by the cross that was later consecrated to Christian worship, that is: the spring dedicated to a Catholic saint?”.
blocks.4: From what has been written, in the sources mentioned above and elsewhere, and from tradition, it must be very likely that this is how the spring got the name it has now, St Olav's spring: it was dedicated to St Olav in early Christian times. The water of the spring is said to have healing powers, and the healing power was said to be especially strong on the eve of St Olav's Day. It is claimed that in heathen times the spring was used to wash the images of the gods. I have also seen it claimed that the sacrificial bowls were washed in water from the spring.
